paragraphs.text: Avatar: The Last Airbender (stylized as Magic: The Gathering | Avatar: The Last Airbender ) is a tentpole set in the Magic: The Gathering Universes Beyond series released by Wizards of the Coast , based on the animated series of the same name . This release was created in collaboration with the creators of Avatar: the Last Airbender , Nickelodeon Animation Studio and its parent company Viacom (Paramount Media Networks) . It was released on November 21, 2025. The set is Standard legal and the 108th Magic expansion.

Avatar: The Last Airbender is a large set with support for Limited play, and is accompanied by other products including a Beginner Box , a Jumpstart release , and a Secret Lair superdrop . It features the new waterbend , earthbend , firebending , and airbend mechanics and makes significant use of Allies and Lessons .
The main Standard -legal set uses the code TLA and features 296 regular cards (91 commons, 110 uncommons, 60 rares, 20 mythic rares, 15 basic lands) . TLA cards are primarily found in booster packs .

Cards not legal in Standard use the set code TLE and an alternate expansion symbol ( ). This group of cards has been officially referred to as " Avatar: The Last Airbender Eternal -legal sets", "Avatar: The Last Airbender Extra", or the "Eternal-Legal Set". Scryfall uses the name "Avatar: The Last Airbender Eternal".
TLE cards are legal in Commander , Legacy , and Vintage , but not Standard. Aside from pre-emptive bans, they are also legal in Timeless and Historic . They are numbered as follows:

Avatar: The Last Airbender is available in Play Boosters , Collector Boosters , a Bundle , a Gift Edition Commander's Bundle , two Scene Boxes , and a Beginner Box . There are also Jumpstart Boosters and 2-Pack Boosters for the accompanying Jumpstart set . It does not feature any Commander decks .

Each Play Booster contains 14 cards and one token or DFC helper card, while each Collector Booster contains 15 cards plus one token or art card . A Play Booster box contains 30 packs, and a Collector Booster box contains 12 packs. Many Booster Fun treatments are exclusive to Collector Boosters, including neon-ink battle pose cards and the raised-foil Avatar Aang . Contents are as follows:

The Avatar: The Last Airbender Beginner Box includes ten themed, 20-card Jumpstart decks (not to be confused with Avatar: The Last Airbender Jumpstart ), two per color . The Aang Tutorial ( ) and Zuko Tutorial ( ) are pre-ordered and guide new players step-by-step through their first game. The other decks are Allies ( ), Spells (noncreature spells, ), Waterbending ( ), Attacking ( ), Counters ( ), Firebending ( ), Earthbending ( ), and Big Creatures ( ). All ten decks, including the tutorials, can be mixed and matched to form 40-card decks.

The Commander's Bundle is a reimagined Gift Edition of the regular Avatar: The Last Airbender Bundle . Apart from an extra Collector Booster , it contains five non-foil promo cards with the TLE expansion code. Three of these promo cards are the same in each Commander's Bundle. These are Avatar: The Last Airbender versions of Sol Ring , Arcane Signet , and Swiftfoot Boots .

The others are 2 of 10 Avatar Commander's Bundle–exclusive Booster Fun cards, which are organized into two cycles. One is a cycle of tutors, the other a cycle of free spells under the condition that you control your commander .
There are also two Scene Boxes each include six borderless scene cards with the TLE expansion code. Each box also includes three Play Boosters, six art cards , and a display easel.

Avatar: The Last Airbender Jumpstart is a supplemental Jumpstart set. Each Jumpstart Booster is a 20-card half-deck containing one of 46 randomly chosen themes; some themes have multiple variants. Any two half-decks can be combined to form a playable 40-card deck.

Traditional foil versions of Avatar: The Last Airbender cards appear in Play and Collector Boosters. The set's Booster Fun treatments include full-art basic lands , extended art cards, elemental frame cards, and several borderless treatments: battle pose (including textless neon-ink), scene cards, field notes, and borderless double-faced Sagas. Avatar Aang // Aang, Master of Elements is the set's headliner , appearing in borderless raised foil . The set also includes a bonus sheet featuring borderless source material cards.

This set's headliner card is Avatar Aang , who transforms into Aang, Master of Elements . The raised foil version, illustrated by Avatar: The Last Airbender co-creator Bryan Konietzko , appears only in English-language Avatar: The Last Airbender Collector Boosters .

The Source Material Cards bonus sheet is a collection of additional cards released alongside the main set. It contains reprinted cards themed for The Last Airbender with stills from the TV series. Play Boosters may contain one of these sixty-one cards with the TLE expansion code. On the Source Material cards, the relevant book and chapter of the original series is indicated in the information below the text box .

The epic showdowns of each book's finale is brought to life on three sets of scene cards. Book 1 is a 4-card scene (#297-300), Book 2 is a 6-card scene (#301-306), and Book 3 is a massive 9-card scene that's befitting of the series finale (#307-315). Book 1, Book 2, and Book 3 scene cards appear in non-foil and traditional foil in Play Boosters and Collector Boosters.
The Last Airbender debuts four new named mechanics, each one corresponding to one of the "bending" styles of the franchise:

Airbend is a keyword action that captures airbending's evasive and disruptive nature. When you airbend a permanent, it is exiled. However, its owner may pay to cast it from exile as long as it is exiled this way. A majority of cards with airbend in this set are white ( ).

Waterbend costs are a new type of cost that appear in activated abilities and as additional costs on spells . They are always generic mana costs. Similarly to convoke and improvise , creatures and artifacts you control can be tapped to pay for in a waterbend cost, flavorfully representing waterbending's focus on tides and change. A majority of cards with waterbend in this set are blue ( ).

Earthbend is a keyword action that symbolizes Earthbenders' strength of taking advantage of the terrain around them. When you earthbend X, target land you control becomes a 0/0 creature with haste in addition to its other types, and you put X +1/+1 counters on it. When that land dies or is exiled, you return it to the battlefield tapped. A majority of cards with earthbend in this set are green ( ).

Firebending is a triggered keyword ability on creatures that represents Firebenders' ability to draw power from aggression. Whenever a creature with firebending X attacks, its controller adds X , which they don't lose between steps and phases until the end of combat. A majority of cards with firebend in this set are red ( ).

Of note, none of the bending mechanics are tied to one specific color , although they are each more prevalent in specific colors, and they each support a variety of mechanical themes in the set rather than being a self-contained theme. This was intentional on the part of Design, who wanted to reflect the versatility of bending as portrayed in the show. Cards with the different bending abilities feature a corresponding watermark .

Exhaust and Flashback are used deciduous mechanics. Clue tokens are created by several cards in the set, although the investigate keyword is not used. Chris Mooney explained that this was done to reduce the number of keywords in the set and to bring Clues more in line with the design of other predefined tokens . The set also includes nonmodal double-faced cards .

The Last Airbender sees the return of the Ally type to Standard, for the first time (outside of reprints) since Oath of the Gatewatch . Ally typal is a major theme of the set. It also introduces the Bison , Lemur , and Platypus creature types.

Lessons return, but mostly for flavor reasons, as there are no cards with the learn mechanic. They constitute a major mechanical theme with many payoffs. Like many Universes Beyond sets before, the set features Sagas ; these depict events within the show's history, and some transform into legendary creatures depicting historical characters. Shrine enchantments also return. The set features one Cave land.
Kangaroo becomes eternal . Mongoose is used on a new card for the first time since Odyssey .
The set introduces conqueror counters for Zhao, the Moon Slayer , and fire counters for Fated Firepower and War Balloon .

The franchise is set in an Asian-inspired fantasy world that is divided into four nations: the Water Tribes, the Fire Nation, the Air Nomads, and the Earth Kingdom. People of each nation are capable of telekinetically manipulating (referred to as "bending" in the franchise) one of the four classical elements : water, earth, fire, or air.

The titular "Avatar" is the only person who can bend all four elements, and they are responsible for maintaining spiritual and physical balance in the world. After an Avatar's death, the Avatar spirit is reborn into a new person of a different nation, who must learn their bending skills anew and take on their Avatar responsibilities.

The scope of this set within the Avatar: The Last Airbender franchise is limited to the original 2005 animated series. The animated series is structured into three seasons, each referred to as a "book", and within each book are individual episodes called "chapters". The three books are titled "Water", "Earth", and "Fire", corresponding to the elements that the titular last Avatar, Aang , must master.

Unusually, the Vision and Set Design teams were led by the same person: Chris Mooney , a subject matter expert in Avatar: The Last Airbender . Designers started with the bending mechanics. They first experimented with a single mechanic to represent all four elements, but found the result boring and repetitive. After some early attempts, they decided that the bending mechanics should be flexible and nonlinear, allowing for creative play patterns. They also wanted the mechanics to be active; a scrapped attempt at firebending , for example, cared about players dealing damage (similar to bloodthirst or spectacle ), which the designers felt was too passive. In Mooney's words, "a Firebender isn't someone who sits around and waits for fire to happen, and then likes it. They're someone who creates and uses fire as a tool."

The focus on the four elements created a color imbalance in the set. Water, fire, and earth mapped easily to blue , red , and green respectively. Air mapped easily to white , but for flavor reasons, it couldn't appear in as high a volume. This left white and black lacking strong mechanical identities. Designers first tried to fill this gap with Spirits , but they didn't feel appropriate in large quantities. Instead, the set ended up with a traditional take on white and black. White represented the world banding together against the Fire Nation, and was made the primary color of Allies . Black represented the show's villains, including but not limited to the Fire Nation.

Firebending was the first mechanic finalized , followed by earthbend , airbend , and waterbend . Clues were added because they worked well with both firebending and waterbend. They were centered in black and mostly flavored as the villains hunting the heroes; the word "investigate" was dropped because it didn't match this flavor. Lessons were the last mechanical theme added, a representation of the main characters' personal growth; learn was omitted to keep the set friendly to new players and for Play Design reasons.

Avatar: The Last Airbender was teased as an "Unannounced Universes Beyond set" on the Announcement Day at MagicCon Las Vegas on October 25, 2024. On January 6, 2025, hints on MTG Arena seemed to indicate that the set would be based on the Avatar: The Last Airbender franchise. On February 21, 2025, the set name was confirmed at the MagicCon Chicago preview panel.
The official debut stream premiered on October 28, 2025. The preview season ran for ten days, after which the full card gallery was revealed on November 7.

Four card cycles associated with the four elements. Each card in the cycle uses the respective watermark .

Besides Aang, the other major characters in the Avatar series also have more than one card. These representations are associated with the character at different points in the story, resulting in a pair or trio of cards. Character growth is represented by increased rarity and sometimes by changed or added colors .

Near the end of the preview season, Tolarian Community College praised Avatar: The Last Airbender for its " Magic -adjacent" setting, the quality of its design , and its full size and support for traditional Booster Draft , while criticizing the source material cards as low-quality collectibles. The review compared Avatar favorably against the recent and poorly received Universes Beyond set Marvel's Spider-Man . Writing for Card Kingdom , Jacob Lackner of Nizzahon Magic gave the set an "B" when ranking 2025's Limited formats, praising the mechanical design, mono-color payoffs, and that all four Bending types were viable in Limited. He criticized that too many cards awarded aggression, resulting in similar feeling decks and games decided in large part by mana curve . At the end of 2025, Mark Rosewater confirmed the set was the second best selling of that year, behind Final Fantasy .
Hasbro latter announced that was the third highest selling in franchise history, trailing only Lord of the Rings and Final Fantasy .
Two cards from Avatar: The Last Airbender , Badgermole Cub and Gran-Gran , were banned from Standard in August 2025, eight months after the set's release.

Badgermole Cub was identified early as one of the most powerful Standard cards on its release, but its fragility kept it from dominating in high level tournaments of the 2025 World Championship , Pro Tour Lorwyn Eclipsed , and Arena Championship 11 before it finally dominated in Pro Tour Secrets of Strixhaven . The most successful builds disregarded its ability to double weaker mana dorks like Spider Manifestation and Gene Pollinator and played bigger landfall plans like Earthbender Ascension . The explosiveness of an unchecked Cub dictated the format's speed, requiring opposing decks to remove the Cub and present game-ending threats with similar speed or get run over. The deck that finally prompted Wizards of the Coast to ban Cub was a green-white shell that played creatures strong against removal like Surrak, Elusive Hunter and Leatherhead, Swamp Stalker , and then quickly ended the game with Practiced Offense . Wizards decided to address the deck with a banning due to its win and play rates, and Cub was chosen as it had high potential to continue dominating the format in other builds.

Avatar also created a new Standard archetype, Izzet Lessons. The deck used Gran-Gran , Combustion Technique , and Accumulate Wisdom as payoffs for running a high Lesson count, and Abandon Attachments , Boomerange Basics , Firebending Lesson , Iroh's Demonstration , and It'll Quench Ya to achieve critical mass. Izzet Lessons was the most played deck of the 2025 World Championships , and won the tournament in the hands of Seth Manfield . A later version of the deck, Jeskai Lessons, incorporated Tablet of Discovery and Jeskai Revelation in a more controlling build. The prominence of Lessons decks led to the banning of Gran-Gran alongside Badgermole Cub. Gran-Gran's ability to filter the deck and provide overwhelming mana acceleration when its set up forced opposing decks to remove it quickly, like Cub. Additionally, four copies of Gran-Gran were usually the only creatures played in these decks, making these removal spells dead cards in many cases. The banning quickly ended the deck's popularity.
Avatar Destiny is the first and currently only Universes Beyond card to be part of a mega cycle .

Earthbending Student appears only in Collector Boosters, only in foil, and only in the single slot that can contain TLE uncommons. For these reasons, as well as the high price of Collector Boosters and the 49 other cards that can appear in the TLE uncommon slot instead, the card is worth an exceptionally high price on the secondary market . It may have been designed as part of the Beginner Box, based on when it was spoiled and on its collector number .
